title: Concurrency + quota patterns and project-key strategy - Hutchinson Data
summary: Demo focused on multi-tenant rate controls, concurrency limits, org vs project API keys, and console patterns for Hutchinson Data. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, sticky routing, token quotas per project, and compliance requirements (SOC2, SSO, audit logs). Agreed next steps: pricing + capacity estimate, security pack, and a short pilot with throughput targets.
next_steps: Redwood to send dedicated capacity estimator and sample pricing by 2025-11-27
Schedule 2-week pilot kickoff with SREs the week of 2025-12-08
Hutchinson to confirm compliance checklist and expected QPS target

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-25
Start time (PST): 15:00
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Rina Shah (Redwood Product), Elena Park (Hutchinson Head of Platform), Daniel Ortiz (CTO), Priya Menon (SRE), Marcus Brown (Legal)
---
Summary auto: walk-through of org/project key model, concurrency/quota patterns, console demo of per-project quotas, and Optimize suggestions for batching/kv cache to save cost.

00:00:03 Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Avery from Redwood, this is Marcus our SE, and Rina from product. Today we'll run through how teams typically map org and project keys and then demo the console and API controls for quotas and throttling, and then leave time for questions. Elena, do you want to kick off with your main goals?

00:00:20 Elena Park: Yeah thanks. Uh so our main thing is we need predictable costs and isolation across multiple product teams. We've run into noisy neighbour issues before where one service spikes and it eats the quota for the org. We're evaluating either a hosted model or dedicated capacity on your side. Security checklist is heavy — SOC2, KMS, SAML SSO — and we've got legal questions about retention.

00:00:42 Marcus Li: Totally, we see that a lot. One of the patterns we recommend is split org key for billing+admin and project keys for team-level isolation, plus per-project concurrency and token quotas. That gives you sticky routing so high-priority projects can be routed to dedicated pools while lower tiers go to burstable capacity.

00:00:58 Daniel Ortiz: Sticky routing? Can you explain that a little, Marcus?

00:01:05 Marcus Li: Sure, sticky routing means requests with a project key can be pinned to a specific capacity pool or model variant. If you set a project to 'dedicated', all traffic bearing that key will prefer the dedicated GPU pool; if capacity full, there's an automatic fallback to a compatible quantized variant in hosted to keep requests alive. It reduces cold migrate thrash and preserves latency SLOs.

00:01:25 Priya Menon: And if the dedicated pool is saturated, does Redwood queue or reject? We need to avoid request storms.

00:01:31 Marcus Li: You can choose behavior per project — queue with backpressure, reject with a 429 and a clear retry-after header, or route to a lower-cost model. We also support token-based quotas and concurrency limits. For example, keep concurrency at N streams per project and a token/month cap.

00:01:50 Elena Park: How granular are these limits? We have teams that need burst capacity for scheduled jobs, but also strict per-team monthly caps.

00:01:58 Rina Shah: In the console you can define policies at org-level, project-level, and key-level. Policies can be rate limits (requests per second), concurrency caps (in-flight requests per key), and budget quotas (tokens per billing period). You can attach schedules — e.g., higher burst windows on weekends — and set automatic escalation to billing if they go over.

00:02:18 Avery Chen: We'll demo that now. Marcus, can you share your screen?

00:02:23 [screen share starts — console appears, slight audio lag]

00:02:30 Marcus Li: Ok here's the org dashboard — you can see active pools, CPU/GPU utilization, and a table of projects. I'm going to open the 'Project controls' for 'search-service' to show policies.

00:02:45 Marcus Li: You see project keys listed, each with its own concurrency limit. This key is set to 20 concurrent streams, token quota 500k/month, and priority 'high'. There's a 'fallback model' set to gptx-compact-8q (note: spoken as "g p t x compact" in transcript).

00:03:05 Elena Park: That model name looks unfamiliar — is that one of your curated variants?

00:03:09 Marcus Li: Yes, it's one of our quantized variants optimized for throughput. Sometimes the transcription will show it oddly, we call it gpt-x-compact-8q internally.

00:03:20 Daniel Ortiz: On billing — if a project hits its token cap mid-month, what's the usual behavior? Do you block, or bill overage?

00:03:28 Avery Chen: It's configurable. Most customers set a soft cap with alerts and a hard cap that blocks. For enterprise contracts there's an option to auto-increase capacity from reserved burst pools with pre-approved billing.

00:03:38 Priya Menon: Do you expose per-key usage streams? We need per-team audit logs because of compliance.

00:03:44 Marcus Li: Yes, token-level audit logs, per-request latency, and tracing hooks are available. You can stream logs to your S3 or SIEM and we support signed audit entries for retention.

00:03:55 Marcus Brown (Legal): And encryption at rest? Key management?

00:03:58 Rina Shah: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for Private deployments and dedicated accounts. Hosted customers can choose our managed KMS or integrate with their cloud KMS through the private plane for the Private offering. We'll attach the SOC2 and KMS integration docs after the call.

00:04:12 [15s silence while Rina pulls doc; slight cross talk]

00:04:30 Marcus Li: Back to throttling patterns — there's a couple of common designs: 1) per-project hard concurrency + token quota, 2) token-bucket smoothing for burst absorb with per-second refill rates, 3) hierarchical quotas where org budget can loan tokens to projects temporarily.

00:04:52 Elena Park: That hierarchical loan model — is it manual or automatic? We want one team to be able to borrow during scheduled jobs, but only if org budget allows.

00:05:00 Marcus Li: It's policy-driven. You can enable 'org borrow' and set rules like max loan percent and payback window. There's also an approval step if loans exceed a threshold — that can route to billing/finance for sign-off.

00:05:12 Daniel Ortiz: I want to understand how this works with KV cache and prefix caching because our embeddings workload benefits a lot from cache hits.

00:05:20 Marcus Li: Good question. We do prefix-based KV caching; cache hits are free-ish because they avoid model compute. The console shows cache hit ratios per-project; Optimize will recommend cache TTLs and chunking strategies based on your token distributions. If you set tight concurrency but high cache hit rates, effective throughput increases without extra cost.

00:05:40 Priya Menon: Any gotchas with token accounting? We need deterministic billing numbers.

00:05:43 Rina Shah: We count input + output tokens per request and expose a billing reconciliation export. For privacy-sensitive customers we can obfuscate payloads but keep token counts. Occasionally transcripts and metric names in exports are noisy — e g, "K V cash" shows up in speech-to-text — but the numeric counters are accurate.

00:06:05 Elena Park: Ok demo the API flow for creating project keys and attaching policies.

00:06:08 Marcus Li: Switching to the API tab — here's a sample cURL: POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/keys with policy block that sets rate_limit: 50 rps, concurrency: 10, token_quota: 1_000_000, fallback_model: "gptx-compact-8q". I'll run one now to create 'etl-service' key.

00:06:30 [keyboard clacking; brief pause]

00:06:35 Marcus Li: OK key created. You can see it in the UI with QR codes for rotation. Rotation is supported via API, and you can set automatic rotation intervals and zero-downtime swaps.

00:06:48 Daniel Ortiz: For the pilot we plan to target 2k rps peak and 120k tokens/minute. Can your dedicated pools handle that consistently?

00:06:58 Marcus Li: We'll size the dedicated pool based on your peak concurrency mix and model selection. For the pilot we'll propose a small dedicated cluster with autoscale headroom and a burst buffer. We'll also run an initial benchmark to validate p95 latency under your workload profile.

00:07:13 Priya Menon: Benchmark — what does Redwood need from us to run that?

00:07:17 Marcus Li: A few things: request shape (avg prompt length, response length), concurrency profile (traffic per minute), and auth keys we can use for a test harness. We'll give a benchmark script that runs from our infra to your projected endpoints.

00:07:29 Elena Park: On telemetry, can we get per-route breakdowns and token-level cost estimates?

00:07:33 Rina Shah: Yes, Console has per-route dashboards and cost attribution by tag. You can map tags to teams and get token spend per tag.

00:07:40 [small interruption, someone drops and rejoins briefly]

00:07:55 Avery Chen: Shifting to common objections — cost vs latency. If you need sub-100ms p95 we recommend small dedicated pools and low-quantization loss models; cost rises, but latency drops. If cost is primary, we recommend alternate quantized variants and batching to amortize overhead. Optimize can analyze transcripts and suggest batch sizes and cache policies.

00:08:22 Elena Park: Is batching supported at the gateway or in the model runtime? We want per-request correlation IDs kept intact.

00:08:28 Marcus Li: Batching happens in the runtime with request-boundary metadata preserved. Correlation IDs are propagated so you can trace individual requests. You can set max batch sizes and max latency thresholds.

00:08:40 Daniel Ortiz: We heard about RBAC per key — can we restrict some keys to only embeddings endpoints?

00:08:45 Rina Shah: Absolutely. Keys can be scoped to endpoints, model families, or tags. You can issue read-only keys for embeddings-only operations.

00:08:54 Priya Menon: Any legal concerns around retention in hosted mode? Our legal prefers Private deployment if retention policies are strict.

00:09:02 Marcus Brown (Legal): Yes, retention + deletion certifications.

00:09:06 Rina Shah: For Private deployments we give a private control plane with full data residency, and we can do on-prem with an air-gapped option. Hosted customers get retention settings and deletion APIs but audit might prefer Private. We'll share the matrix in a table.

00:09:22 Elena Park: Great. Any quick demo of Optimize suggestions?

00:09:26 Marcus Li: Sure — switching to Optimize. It shows a heatmap of requests by prompt length and suggests quantization for long-response tasks and batching for short prompts. For your search-service it recommends increasing prefix cache TTL to 48h and a batch window of 80ms to reduce per-token cost by ~22% given your forecast.

00:09:48 Elena Park: Sounds helpful. Ok — last question: what's the recommended key rotation period? We rotate monthly for API keys.

00:09:55 Marcus Li: Monthly is fine. For high-security keys we recommend weekly rotation and use of KMS-based wrapping so you can revoke quickly.

00:10:03 Daniel Ortiz: Alright. Let's recap next steps.

00:10:07 Avery Chen: Recap: Redwood sends a tailored pricing + dedicated capacity estimate, SOC2/KMS docs, benchmark script, and an SOW draft. Hutchinson shares traffic shapes, current token metrics, and compliance checklist. Schedule pilot kickoff the week of 2025-12-08.

00:10:24 Elena Park: That works. Thanks everyone.

00:10:28 Marcus Brown: We'll review T&Cs internally and come back with legal questions.

00:10:33 Avery Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up via email with attachments and a calendar invite for the pilot planning slot.

00:10:38 [meeting ends — 58 minutes total, remaining time used for offline Q/A between Marcus Li and Priya on one-off SRE edge cases]

---
Notes about transcript quality: speaker labels occasionally mismatched; some product names transcribed oddly (gptx-compact-8q -> g p t x compact), KV cache transcribed as "K V cash". Numbers and policy fields presented in console logs are accurate in the recording but may be imprecise in speech-to-text.
